title: SLO-tiered lossy proxy for cache and stream dependencies
creator: Asha Kapoor
description:
Problem: during regional surge and degraded downstream capacity (Redis/Kafka/Postgres replicas) we frequently exhaust connection budgets and see cascading tail latency that violates 99th pct SLOs. Existing mitigations (aggressive hedging, admission, and fallback proxies) work but are blunt and either waste resources or surface stale/incomplete results to customers with little control per-SLO tier.

Goal: implement a lightweight, SLO-aware 'lossy proxy' that sits in front of stateful dependencies (cache and stream consumers) to apply graded, content-aware degradation and admission controls. The proxy will provide fine-grained controls per-SLO tier and route: for caches it can do TTL relaxation, sampled partial-serve, or folded-key fallbacks; for streams it can do batch truncation, earliest-offset-skipping, or compacted-snapshot responses. The proxy's job is not to replace connpool or circuit breakers, but to complement them by reducing downstream load in predictable ways that align with business SLOs and per-route importance.

Scope: prototype proxy for Redis (GET/LPUSH patterns) and Kafka consumer APIs used by the runtime request path. Integrations: Redwood routing layer, Console feature-flag + rollout, and observability (per-proxy metrics and traces).

Non-goals: rewriting consumer code to be idempotent or changing Kafka retention policies; replacing existing circuit-breaker or admission-limits (we integrate with them).
acceptance_criteria: Proxy can be inserted as a sidecar or regional edge service and configured per-route with SLO tier rules
Metrics emitted: admitted_requests, shed_requests, partial_serves, ttl_relaxations, truncated_batches, avg_latency_by_tier (30s/5m/1h)

End-to-end experiment: under simulated 30% downstream capacity degradation, high-priority routes maintain 99th latency SLO <= target while low-priority routes degrade gracefully with measurable cost reduction
Canary rollout with automated rollback via Console if proxy increases P95 or error-rate for any high-priority route by >10%
Documentation and runbook published in Confluence and linked in Console rollout panel
Automated chaos test (k-sim) that simulates Redis slow responses and Kafka broker retirements reproduces expected shedding behavior and logs decision traces
implementation_notes: Design: proxy configuration model should be a declarative policy: matchers (route, tenant, region), slo_tier, actions (ttl_relax(ms), sample_rate, partial_serve_keyset, truncate_batch(n), fallback_variant)

Integrate with existing admission controller: proxy queries token-bucket tokens before applying heavy prefetches; if admission rejected, proxy immediately applies most aggressive degrade action for that tier
Work with runtime team to add lightweight decision-tracing headers so downstream calls can be correlated with Console traces
Proxy should favor predictable CPU/memory usage. For Redis partial-serve, implement a streaming multi-get with early-return heuristics to avoid head-of-line amplification
For Kafka: implement batch prefetch with maximum fetched-records cap and optional snapshotting for compaction-enabled topics
Enable policy overrides per-tenant via Console (enterprise-only) and default conservative policies for self-serve accounts
rollout_plan: Stage 1 (canary): deploy in us-east-1 behind a feature flag for 5% of requests for non-critical routes. Monitor admitted/shed ratios and latency (48h)
Stage 2 (region incremental): expand to us-west-2 and eu-west-1 for a subset of tenants with low traffic; run load tests that simulate Redis latency inflation and Kafka broker churn
Stage 3 (per-route enforcement): enable per-route SLO tiers with default actions; enable console controls for ops to tweak live
Rollback criteria: any sustained (>15m) P95 increase above 10% or error-rate spike >5x baseline for high-priority routes
Post-rollout: bake for 2 weeks, run a full incident drill that triggers proxy shedding and validate customer-impact metrics
tests_and_simulation: Unit tests for policy evaluation and action ordering (ttl_relax before sample when both allowed)
Integration: end-to-end test harness using localstack-like tooling for Kafka + embedded Redis to validate truncation and partial-serve correctness
Chaos tests: introduce artificial 200-500ms per-request Redis delay and random 5-10% Kafka broker timeouts to verify shed behavior
Performance: benchmark proxy overhead under 10k RPS with various policies; target <3% median added latency for admitted requests
SLO validation: synthetic load test that asserts high-priority route still meets SLO while low-priority reduces token consumption by >=35%
observability_and_alerting: Dashboards: per-region, per-tier panels showing admitted vs shed, cost-per-request (tokens), avg latency by tier
Tracing: decision trace ID passed as x-redwood-proxy-decision for correlation with request traces
Alerts: alert on shed_rate > 50% for any high-priority route or error_rate increase > 2x after a config change
Audit logs: record policy evaluation outcomes and tenant overrides to support post-mortem analysis

2026-02-20 - Liam O'Neill: Raised concern about correctness for partial-serve on complex object graphs; suggestion: prefer compacted snapshots for multi-key reads when consistency is required.
2026-02-27 - Diego M: Prototype bench (local) shows 40% reduction in Redis QPS for low-tier routes with TTL relaxation + sampling combo. Sharing perf artifacts in Drive.
